Babylon. One of the ancient world's greatest cities, Babylon was the political and cultural center of successive empires in Mesopotamia, most prominently during the reigns of Hammurabi in the eighteenth century BCE and Nebuchadnezzar the Second in the early sixth century BCE. Situated on the Euphrates River in what is now Iraq, Babylon served as a hub of trade, learning, administration, and religious authority, home to the temples of the god Marduk and birthplace of sophisticated systems of law, astronomy, and mathematics.

Babylon emerged as a city-state around the eighteenth century BCE under Hammurabi, who conquered surrounding territories and established the Babylonian Empire. Under Hammurabi, Babylon became the paramount power in Mesopotamia, known for centralized administration and codified law. The Code of Hammurabi, created around seventeen fifty-four BCE, was one of history's earliest comprehensive legal codes, erected as a stone pillar in Babylon. It established principles of justice, property, commerce, and crime that influenced subsequent legal systems across the ancient world.

Babylon declined after Hammurabi's reign but was conquered and restored by the Kassite dynasty and later by the Assyrian Empire. It was then re-established as a great power under Nebuchadnezzar the Second from six hundred five to five hundred sixty-two BCE, who rebuilt the city to monumental grandeur. Under Nebuchadnezzar the Second, Babylon reached its architectural and political height. The city featured the Ishtar Gate, dedicated to the goddess of love and war, with glazed brick walls depicting bulls and dragons, and the famous Hanging Gardens, one of the Seven Wonders of the Ancient World, though archaeological evidence remains debated.

The Tower of Babel, mentioned in biblical tradition, may be an echo of or confusion with Babylon's Etemenanki, a great temple tower dedicated to Marduk. The ziggurat was the religious center of the city and a marvel of ancient engineering. Babylon served as a center of mathematics, astronomy, and cuneiform scholarship. Babylonian astronomers developed sophisticated understanding of celestial bodies and created predictions of lunar and solar phenomena that influenced later Greek astronomy.

The city's position on the Euphrates made it a crucial trade hub connecting the Persian Gulf to regions further west. Babylon controlled overland trade routes and river commerce, accumulating wealth and cultural influence. It fell to the Persian Empire under Cyrus the Second in five hundred thirty-nine BCE and later came under the control of successive empires. Its decline was gradual, and by the medieval period it had been abandoned and eventually lost to the sands. In Judeo-Christian tradition, Babylon became a symbol of worldly power, excess, and divine judgment, particularly after its conquest of Judea and the deportation of Jews in five hundred eighty-six BCE.
